Adaptive landscapes

Source: R/landscape.R
landscapes.Rd

A landscape is a function taking a matrix of phenotypes (one row per individual) and returning a vector of fitness values. Any such function can be used directly; these constructors cover the common cases.

Usage

landscape_perlin(
  frequency,
  seed,
  offset = 0,
  transform = function(z) (z + 1)/2,
  dim = 2,
  ...
)

landscape_gaussian(optima, omega = 1, heights = 1, combine = c("sum", "max"))

landscape_smoothmax(..., beta = 100)

landscape_function(f, dim)

landscape_grid(landscape, lower = 0, upper = 15, step = 0.005)

Arguments

frequency

Perlin frequency; higher values give more rugged landscapes.

seed

Perlin seed.

offset

Added to phenotypes before evaluating the noise (scalar or one value per dimension), e.g. to shift the landscape off the lattice.

transform

Applied to the raw noise in \([-1, 1]\); the default rescales to \([0, 1]\).

dim

Number of phenotypic dimensions.

...

Further arguments to `ambient::gen_perlin()`.

optima

Matrix of peak positions, one row per peak.

omega

Width of the peaks: scalar variance, vector of variances, or a covariance matrix (shared by all peaks), or a list of matrices.

heights

Peak heights.

combine

`"sum"` or `"max"` over peaks.

beta

Sharpness; large values approach the maximum.

f

Function taking a phenotype matrix and returning fitness values.

landscape

A 2D landscape to cache.

lower, upper

Grid bounds (scalar or per dimension).

step

Grid spacing.

Functions

  • landscape_perlin(): Perlin noise (via the ambient package), in 2 or 3 dimensions.

  • landscape_gaussian(): Sum (or maximum) of Gaussian peaks, \(W(x) = \sum_k h_k \exp(-\frac12 (x-\theta_k)^\top \Omega^{-1} (x-\theta_k))\).

  • landscape_smoothmax(): Smooth maximum of several landscapes, \(\sum_k w_k e^{\beta w_k} / \sum_k e^{\beta w_k}\).

  • landscape_function(): Wrap any function of a phenotype matrix.

  • landscape_grid(): Precompute a 2D landscape on a grid and interpolate bilinearly. Much faster for landscapes that are slow to evaluate (e.g. Perlin noise, where each call has a large fixed cost), at the price of a small interpolation error. Outside the grid, values are clamped to the nearest edge.
